name: PT Arwana Citramulia Tbk
industry_name: Industrial goods, building products & electrical equipment

frontmatter.title: Arwana Citramulia: a cash-generative tile leader priced for no growth
frontmatter.summary: Initiation at BUY with a Rp829 target. Arwana makes about a seventh of Indonesia's ceramic tiles from five plants running at near-full utilisation, earns a mid-twenties return on equity, holds net cash and pays out 69.4% to 71.6% of profit, rising to 79.0% in FY2025. At 6.6x forward earnings the market pays nothing for the recovery already visible in the nine-month accounts.
thesis: The market extrapolates the FY2023-FY2025 margin slide into perpetuity: at 6.6x FY2026E earnings and 3.9x EV/EBITDA the price implies flat revenue forever, while nine-month revenue is up and gross margin has already recovered to 31.7% [S2, S0].

Capacity, not price, is the growth engine from here: 75 million square metres of installed capacity against 68.0 million square metres sold in FY2025, and the Ogan Ilir expansion adds a new porcelain line into the upper-mid segment [S4].

Distribution and utilisation are the moat: 56 sub-distributors served by our own distribution subsidiary, seven more than a year earlier, with tens of thousands of stores behind them, and 97% of capacity used against an industry at 73% [S4].

Cash conversion, not accounting profit, is the reason to own it: operating cash flow exceeded net profit in FY2025, the balance sheet is net cash, and the dividend and the buy-back are both funded by cash rather than by leverage [S3, S2, S0].

The bear case is a governance one, not a demand one: IDR2,427.0bn of FY2025 sales went to related parties, and the discount will not close until that channel is priced as a permanent minority risk [S3].

catalysts.event: FY2026 results: first full year with the {{fact.F7|num0}} million square metres capacity base and, we expect, a fourth consecutive quarter of seasonally strong sales
Annual general meeting and FY2026 dividend declaration, the payout decision that sets the cash return for the year
Government decision on the HGBT gas-price volume quota, the largest single input-cost variable for the tile industry
Housing-programme target for the new year and the first-quarter order flow from the three-million-homes pipeline
Full-year ASAKI utilisation data and the trade ministry's stance on the ceramic import safeguard

blocks.text: We initiate Arwana Citramulia at **BUY** with a twelve-month target of Rp829, 64.1% above the Rp505 price and 76.2% including the Rp61 of dividends we expect over the next twelve months. The company is a five-plant ceramic-tile producer with 75 million square metres of installed capacity, about a seventh of national output, running its lines at 97% utilisation while the industry averages 73.0%; it carries net cash and has paid out 69.4% to 71.6% of its earnings through FY2024, rising to 79.0% in FY2025 [S4, S3, S0].

The variant view is narrow and specific. The market treats the FY2023-FY2025 gross-margin decline from 36.9% to 30.3% as permanent and pays 6.6x forward earnings for a business that has already reversed it. Nine-month revenue of IDR2,512.4bn is up on the prior year, gross profit of IDR796.1bn is a 31.7% margin, and profit attributable to owners of IDR369.6bn is running well ahead of the IDR302.1bn earned in the same period of the prior year [S2]. That is not a forecast; it is in the accounts.

Three things move the value. First, the mix: rectified tiles went from about three-tenths to 46.0% of production, and that is what lifted average selling prices faster than gas and clay costs [S4]. Second, the demand base: the three-million-homes programme had delivered 1.79m units by mid-October, and the annual report argues that full delivery would push national utilisation toward the level at which price competition fades [S4, S8]. Third, the cash return: at Rp505 the stock yields 12.0% forward on a 79.0% payout, and the model carries net cash of IDR-274.5bn by our FY2026E year-end, with a buy-back that has been running at about one per cent of the shares a year [S2, S0].

What we are not claiming is that the discount is irrational. IDR2,427.0bn of FY2025 sales, more than four-fifths of the total, went to related parties, with a single related-party customer at roughly two-thirds of net sales [S3]. A minority holder is buying a business whose revenue depends on counterparties controlled by the same key management, and no valuation removes that. We price it three ways: a governance premium in the discount rate, a bear case in which the affiliate takes five points of gross margin, and cross-check multiples at the peer median rather than at a premium.

Arwana Citramulia manufactures and distributes ceramic floor and wall tiles, including rectified and large-format porcelain, under the Arwana, UNO and Gloria brands. Production runs from five plants — Pasar Kemis and Serang in Banten, Cikande in West Java, Gresik in East Java and Ogan Ilir in South Sumatra — with installed capacity of 75 million square metres a year in 2026 after the Ogan Ilir expansion, against 66.9 million square metres produced and 68.0 million square metres sold in FY2025 [S4]. The company is a manufacturer first and a brand second: its own distribution subsidiary, PT Primagraha Keramindo, is the sole distributor of the group's output and is connected to 56 sub-distributors in the major cities and to tens of thousands of stores across the archipelago, including a modern-trade presence through the Gloria brand [S3, S4].

The revenue model is simple and cyclical. Volume follows housing completions and renovation demand; price follows the mix between standard, rectified and large-format porcelain. The company does not publish quarterly volumes, but the annual report is explicit that the conversion of standard lines to rectified output — from about three-tenths to 46.0% of production — is what drove average selling prices above input-cost inflation in FY2025 [S4]. Capacity utilisation of 97% against an industry at 73% is the operational signature of a cost leader: fixed costs spread over more square metres than any domestic peer [S4].

Strategy has three legs. The first is capacity: the new line at Ogan Ilir adds just over five million square metres a year of new capacity with large-format porcelain capability, aimed at commercial projects, shopping centres and vertical housing that the company could not serve before [S4]. The second is mix: the Gloria brand and the rectified conversion move the product away from the price-sensitive bottom of the market, which is where imported tiles compete hardest [S4, S6]. The third is distribution: the sub-distributor network grew by seven in 2025, to 56, with the seven new houses spread from North Sumatra to Central Papua, and that is the asset that lets a plant in South Sumatra reach the whole archipelago [S4].

The competitive position is leader among listed peers but not dominant in the industry: 66.9 million square metres of production against 672 million square metres of national capacity running at 73.0% is roughly a seventh of national output, and the industry is fragmented across private producers as well as listed ones [S4, S5]. Being the lowest-cost, highest-utilisation producer in a fragmented, oversupplied industry is a real advantage, but it is an advantage in cost and distribution rather than in pricing power.

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Founder and chief executive Tandean Rustandy holds a controlling stake directly, insiders together hold 61.3%, and the free float is 32.0% [S4, S0]. There is no conglomerate parent: Arwana is a standalone family-controlled manufacturer rather than a member of a group, and the exchange registry does not place it on the high-shareholding-concentration list [S4, konglo registry]. The board is chaired by a former military officer and the founding family supplies the chief executive, the finance director and the operating director [S4].

Customers are the part of the business a new owner must understand first. Sales to related parties were IDR2,427.0bn in FY2025, more than four-fifths of consolidated net sales, and the single largest customer — itself a related party — accounted for IDR1,981.8bn, roughly two-thirds of net sales [S3]. The group's explanation is that it sells through affiliated distribution companies controlled by the same key management, at prices and terms also available to third parties, and the auditor tested the arrangement as a key audit matter rather than qualifying it [S3]. We treat the channel as real — the cash arrives and related-party receivables fell in FY2025 — but as a structural governance discount, discussed in section six.

Indonesia's ceramic-tile industry is large, domestic and structurally long. National capacity is projected at 672 million square metres in 2026 and is expected to grow at a similar pace to 2029, while ASAKI reports that almost all of national production is absorbed by the domestic market [S5]. Utilisation rose from about two-thirds in 2024 to 73.0% in 2025, the first meaningful improvement in years, but that still leaves roughly a quarter of the installed base idle [S4, S5]. The industry is therefore not short of capacity; it is short of demand, and the whole investment case rests on whether demand growth outruns the capacity being added.

The demand drivers are housing and, to a lesser extent, renovation. The three-million-homes programme is the largest single swing factor: 1.79m units had been realised by 15 October 2026, and the annual report states that full delivery would lift national tile utilisation toward full utilisation, a level at which the price competition that has squeezed margins for three years would ease [S4, S8]. The programme is subsidised and therefore less sensitive to mortgage rates than the commercial market, which matters while the policy rate is held high, but its execution has been slower than the headline target [S8].

Supply-side policy is the second driver, and it currently favours domestic producers. The industry operates behind a combination of anti-dumping duties on Chinese ceramic imports, mandatory Indonesian national standards for imported tiles, a specific gas price for industry and a safeguard duty, all of which the company lists as the reason domestic utilisation improved while other manufacturing sectors weakened [S4, S6]. The ministry has been explicit that protection should be temporary and measured, and a review of the policy mix notes that protection only works while domestic producers use the breathing space to become competitive [S6]. A safeguard that lapses, or an anti-dumping duty that is not renewed, is the fastest way for the import channel to reopen.

Input costs are the third driver and the hardest to forecast. Gas is the dominant energy cost in tile firing, and the industry operates under the HGBT scheme, which caps the price for certain industrial users. The scheme has been extended, but the volume quota allocated to each industry was still unresolved in November 2026, with the industry association asking for certainty on supply as well as price [S7]. Our base case assumes the price cap continues and the quota is not cut; that is the policy of record, not an assumption of generosity.

The macro backdrop is neutral-to-negative for a domestic building-materials name. The house macro deck holds Indonesian growth near trend, sees inflation contained and expects the rupiah to weaken further against the dollar; rate-sensitive domestic demand is the category the macro desk avoids, and building materials sits inside that sensitivity through the property cycle [S0]. A weak rupiah raises the cost of imported raw material and of imported competing tiles at the same time, which cuts both ways: it protects share and it raises cost.

Five forces, briefly. Rivalry is high: 672 million square metres of capacity against demand that utilises 73.0% of it means price is the marginal competitor's tool. Buyer power is high and rising, because modern trade and the large distributors consolidate purchasing and because the largest customer is an affiliate [S3]. Supplier power is moderate: gas is regulated, clay is domestic and abundant, and scale gives the company a procurement advantage [S4]. The threat of new entry is low at the low end, where utilisation is poor, and moderate at the porcelain end, where the company itself is investing. Substitution is real but slow: vinyl and homogeneous tile take share at the bottom, granite and large-format porcelain take it at the top, which is where Arwana is moving [S4].

The moat, such as it is, is distribution density plus cost position. A network of 56 sub-distributors reached through a dedicated distribution subsidiary, seven more than a year earlier and still expanding into secondary cities, is what lets a five-plant producer serve islands that smaller competitors cannot reach economically; 97% utilisation is what lets it absorb fixed costs at a level the industry average cannot match [S4]. That is enough to justify a decade of above-cost returns in a discounted cash flow, but not enough to justify a premium multiple: the industry's history is one of price wars that periodically reset margins, and our terminal assumptions fade the return on new capital to about sixteen per cent against an 11.7% cost of capital rather than holding today's rate forever [S0, S4].

The five-year record is a margin story wrapped around a growth story. Revenue rose from IDR2,586.7bn in FY2022 to IDR2,914.3bn in FY2025, but gross margin fell from 40.7% to 30.3% over the same period as gas and raw-material costs rose faster than prices [S0, S3]. Operating margin compressed from 28.9% to 18.1%, and net profit attributable to owners fell to IDR400.5bn despite the higher revenue [S0]. FY2025 was also a year of missed targets: volume of 68.0 m m2 million square metres came in roughly eight percent below the 73.7 m m2 million square metres plan, and net profit missed the internal target by about fifteen percent [S4].

The reported figures need one correction before they can be used. The data pack carries a depreciation charge of a few billion rupiah for FY2025, a fraction of the real figure; the audited accounts show total depreciation of IDR128.4bn in FY2025 and IDR111.9bn in FY2024, allocated across manufacturing overhead, general and administrative expense and selling expense [S3, S9]. We restate the last four years from the filings — IDR96.5bn in FY2022 and IDR112.6bn in FY2023 — and the engine rebuilds EBITDA from them, so FY2025 EBITDA is IDR656.5bn rather than the IDR528.1bn of operating profit plus a token charge as the raw data implies [S3, S9, S10]. Revenue, cost of sales and capex in the pack reconcile to the audited statements, so the restatement is confined to depreciation.

The 2026 recovery is the reason the estimates exist at all. Nine-month revenue of IDR2,512.4bn compares with IDR2,173.9bn in the same period of 2025, a high-teens increase carried by a record third quarter; gross profit of IDR796.1bn is a 31.7% margin against 30.3% for the whole of FY2025; and profit attributable to owners of IDR369.6bn is well ahead of the IDR302.1bn of the prior period [S2]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of IDR3,482.6bn, EBITDA of IDR848.0bn and net profit to owners of IDR535.1bn, which requires only that the fourth quarter repeats the third rather than beating it [S2, S0].

The revenue build from FY2027E is capacity-led. Installed capacity of 75 million square metres against 68.0 million square metres sold leaves room for volume growth without new capital, and we add roughly four percent of volume a year plus a mix contribution from rectified and porcelain output, giving revenue growth of 7.5% in FY2027E and fading to 5.5% by FY2030E [S4, S5]. The four percent is the honest reading of the headroom: 75 million square metres at the 97% utilisation the company actually ran in FY2025 is about seven percent more production than it sold, and two years of four percent absorbs the new line without assuming a utilisation rate the company has not already demonstrated [S4, S0]. That is deliberately below the 2026 rate: the recovery year is a mix and price event, and a second year of high-teens growth would require the housing programme to deliver at a pace it has not yet shown [S8].

Margins are held at the last actual rather than projected upward. Gross margin stays at 31.7% through FY2028E and eases to 31.5% by FY2030E, which is above the FY2025 trough of 30.3% and far below the FY2023 actual of 36.9% and the FY2022 peak of 40.7% [S0]. We do not lift the base above today's margin even though the third quarter printed above it on a mix that is still improving, because the five-year record is a ten-point decline from peak to trough and the operating leverage that produced the recovery works in both directions; the upside from a return to the FY2023 margin is quantified in the bull case rather than assumed here. Operating expenses run at IDR409.2bn, in line with the current run-rate, and the effective tax rate stays at the FY2025 level, IDR117.7bn on IDR523.6bn of pre-tax profit [S3].

Cash flow is the strongest part of the record. FY2025 operating cash flow of IDR667.0bn was well above net profit, because working capital released as receivables and inventories fell, and capex of IDR305.5bn left free cash flow of IDR351.1bn in a year when the company was building the Ogan Ilir line [S3, S0]. Working capital of IDR384.2bn compares with IDR503.0bn a year earlier, a substantial release [S0]. The balance sheet carries IDR73.0bn of debt against IDR377.9bn of cash, a net cash position, and minority interests of IDR37.9bn that represent the stake in the distribution subsidiary that is not owned [S0, S3].

The capex path is where the forecast is most exposed to one project. Nine-month capex is well below the full-year forecast of IDR330.8bn because the plant still under construction at Ogan Ilir is scheduled for completion in December 2026, and the September accounts carry it as work in progress at between three-quarters and four-fifths complete [S2]. The completion payment therefore lands in the fourth quarter, which is why we hold capex at 9.5% of sales for the year rather than annualising the nine-month run-rate, and why FY2027E steps down to 9.0% [S2, S4].

Capital allocation is shareholder-friendly and consistent. The FY2025 dividend was Rp45 a share against earnings of Rp57, a 79.0% payout — the first year above three quarters after three years between 69.4% and 71.6% — and it was paid in 2026, after the balance-sheet date. The IDR303.8bn in the FY2025 cash-flow statement is therefore not that distribution but the FY2024 dividend of Rp43 a share paid in April 2025, which the model carries on that cash basis [S2, S3, S11, S0]. Share count has fallen through treasury buy-backs — from IDR7,271.2bn in FY2022 to IDR7,030.0bn in FY2025 — and capex is funded from operating cash flow with no new borrowing in any year of the history [S0]. We model a Rp61 dividend for FY2026E at 79.0% of earnings and a share count that changes by -1.1% a year, the realised rate: at those rates FY2027E earnings per share of Rp84 rise 8.8% on net profit of IDR575.6bn against IDR535.1bn, and the gap is the buy-back [S2, S0].

Earnings quality, on the house screens, is better than the governance headline suggests. Accruals are negative — operating cash flow exceeds net profit in every year of the history — receivables fell while revenue rose in FY2025, and inventories fell by nearly a third [S0]. There is no special-monitoring-board status, no special notation, no going-concern language and no late filing; the auditor is a member firm of Ernst & Young and issued an unmodified opinion with revenue recognition as a key audit matter [S3]. The one flag that matters is related-party gravity: IDR2,427.0bn of related-party revenue and IDR802.7bn of related-party receivables, the latter equal to more than a quarter of total assets, is the modal value-transfer channel on this exchange and must be watched quarterly [S3]. We classify it as an optics-class flag — disclosed, audited and priced — rather than a manipulation-class one, but it is the reason the multiples we apply to the cross-checks are not premium ones.

We value Arwana on a discounted cash flow as the primary method, with P/E and EV/EBITDA as cross-checks. The DCF fits because the company is a mature, dividend-paying, asset-intensive manufacturer whose value rests on the spread between return on capital and cost of capital rather than on a single commodity price; there is no exchange-traded benchmark for ceramic tiles, so no commodity deck applies [S0, S4]. The multiples are included to keep the DCF honest: they show what the market pays today and what a buyer of the earnings stream would pay without relying on a ten-year forecast [S0].

The cost of capital comes out at 11.7% for an essentially all-equity balance sheet, and the build reproduces. The starting point is the 7.4% rupiah risk-free rate, from which the engine deducts the 1.6% Indonesia default spread, because the local risk-free rate and the country premium both already contain sovereign risk and deducting it is the house convention against double counting. It then adds 0.80 of unlevered beta — the industry median from the betas file — multiplied by the sum of the 4.2% mature-market equity risk premium and the 2.5% Indonesian country premium, and finally the 0.5% governance premium this company carries. That gives a cost of equity of 11.7%; with debt at 0.1% of the capital structure and a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, the weighted average is 11.7% [S0]. It sits inside the eleven-to-thirteen per cent house band for rupiah names, and the governance premium is what keeps it off the floor: an eighty-three per cent related-party revenue channel audited as a key audit matter is not a risk beta captures, and the report would be dishonest if it claimed a discount rate that priced something it did not [S3].

The DCF produces Rp883 a share, with 52.2% of the value in the terminal period. The explicit forecast carries free cash flow from the 2026 recovery through a decade of mid-single-digit growth. The fade is explicit in the reinvestment: in the terminal year capex of IDR446.6bn against depreciation of IDR268.0bn and a working-capital build of IDR31.7bn is roughly a quarter of that year's after-tax operating profit, so at 4.0% terminal growth the return on new capital is about sixteen per cent against the 11.7% discount rate [S0]. That is a fade, not a perpetuity of today's return: we hold the mid-twenties return on capital earned now only through the explicit period, and let new capital earn a spread over cost of capital rather than the whole of today's excess return. We do not fade all the way to the cost of capital because the moat is named and measurable — utilisation of 97% against an industry at 73%, and a sub-distributor network that grew by seven in a single year, to 56 — and a full fade would require evidence that advantage is eroding, which the 2026 accounts do not show [S4].

The two cross-checks disagree with the DCF, and the disagreement is the thesis. P/E at 9.7x earnings gives Rp648, -26.6% versus the DCF. EV/EBITDA at 5.6x gives Rp538, -39.0%, and this is the one number in the report we do not defend: it divides the data pack's last-twelve-month EBITDA, which still carries the truncated depreciation charge section three restates out of the income statement, so it capitalises something close to operating profit. The engine's restatement hook would fix the charge only by replacing the entire last-twelve-month block — including September-2026 net profit, a fifth above the last audited year — with FY2025, which would understate the P/E cross-check by more than it corrected here. We therefore leave the market metric as the pack carries it and treat the result as a floor; on the restated charge the same multiple lifts the cross-check by about a fifth, which moves the target by less than two percent and changes no conclusion [S0, S3]. Both multiples are drawn from a peer and history set that includes years when the stock traded at twice today's rating, and they land far below the DCF because the earnings base they capitalise is depressed. We keep the house weights of 60% DCF, 25% P/E and 15% EV/EBITDA, which produces the Rp829 target. A reader who believes the multiple never re-rates should use the P/E cross-check, and the bear case is built to show what that looks like [S0].

The growth arithmetic is checkable, and it is the method card's test. Return on equity in FY2026E is 26.7% and return on invested capital is in the mid-twenties, so four-to-five percent growth needs a reinvestment rate of roughly a quarter of net operating profit; capex of IDR330.8bn against depreciation of IDR153.2bn and working capital of IDR459.7bn delivers it without straining the balance sheet [S0, S3]. At the margin the terminal year is consistent: a quarter of NOPAT reinvested for four percent growth is a sixteen per cent incremental return, which is what a fragmented industry should be allowed to earn, not the twenty-two per cent that a lower capex assumption would have capitalised in perpetuity.

One thing the DCF does embed, and we say so rather than dress it up: the terminal value is struck on a normalised FY2035 and, divided by that year's EBITDA of IDR1,356.6bn, implies an exit multiple above today's 5.0xx on last-twelve-month EBITDA and above the 3.9xx forward rating. That is multiple expansion in cash-flow clothing. It is defensible only because the terminal year's EBITDA is a normalised one at a 19.5% operating margin rather than today's depressed base, and the exit multiple implied is roughly where the stock traded through FY2022-FY2024; a reader who refuses to pay any re-rating should weight the P/E cross-check at Rp648 instead of the blended target [S0].

A reader who thinks the excess return fades all the way to the cost of capital by the end of the explicit period should read the two no-moat values instead of the grid: the P/E cross-check at Rp648 and the bear case at Rp561. Both are what the stock is worth with no perpetual spread at all, both sit within a tenth of today's price, and the gap between them and the Rp883 DCF is therefore the entire value of the moat we claim. That is the honest way to size the terminal-return bet: it is worth roughly a third of the target, not the whole of it [S0, S4].

What today's price implies is the cleanest way to state the mispricing. Running the DCF backwards at the Rp505 price solves for revenue growth of -2.0% in FY2027E and below our terminal assumption thereafter, holding our margins and cost of capital: the market is paying for a business that never grows again, at the very moment the accounts show it growing at a high-teens rate [S2, S0]. That is not a claim that the market is irrational — a related-party-dominated revenue base and a market that has de-rated small caps indiscriminately are reasons to demand a discount — but it is a claim that the discount is larger than the operating risk justifies.

The largest risk is that the 2026 recovery is a price event that reverses. Gross margin went from 30.3% to 31.7% on mix and on a housing programme that has delivered 1.79m units against an annual target of three million; if completions stall, volume and price fall together, which is precisely the bear case [S4, S8]. Likelihood medium, impact high, because the operating leverage that produced the recovery works in both directions.

The second risk is input cost. Gas is regulated through HGBT and the scheme has been extended, but the volume quota for industrial users was still unresolved in November 2026 and the industry association has warned that price certainty without supply certainty is not enough [S7]. A cut in the quota, or a rise in the administered price, hits the cost base directly and cannot be passed through quickly in a market where the marginal competitor sets price. Likelihood medium, impact high.

The third risk is trade policy. Anti-dumping duties on Chinese tiles, mandatory national standards and a safeguard duty are the stated reason domestic utilisation improved, and the industry ministry has described protection as temporary [S4, S6]. If the safeguard lapses or enforcement weakens, imported tiles re-enter at prices the domestic cost base cannot match. Likelihood medium, impact high.

The fourth risk is governance and related-party dependence, and it is the one the model now prices three ways. IDR2,427.0bn of sales to related parties and a single related-party customer at IDR1,981.8bn mean the revenue line depends on pricing decisions between entities controlled by the same key management, and IDR802.7bn of related-party receivables is a claim on those same entities [S3]. We found no evidence of diversion — the auditor tested the arrangement, the receivables fell in FY2025, and cash conversion is strong — so the base case prices the flows at the terms the accounts describe, and the exposure is carried in three named places: a 0.5% governance premium in the discount rate, the bear case's five-point gross-margin shift, and cross-check multiples at the peer median rather than at a premium. The size of that lever is worth stating plainly: five points of gross margin on FY2026E revenue of IDR3,482.6bn takes about a quarter of FY2026E operating profit of IDR694.8bn — a sixth of the IDR1,104.0bn gross-profit line — and that is what a transfer-pricing affiliate could take without changing a single invoice date [S3, S0]. Likelihood of a value-damaging related-party event low, impact high.

The fifth set of risks is financial and market-structural. The balance sheet is net cash, so solvency is not a risk in any plausible scenario; but the stock is small, with a free float of 32.0% and thin daily turnover, and the Indonesian market has been de-rating small caps through 2026 while the index provider consults on reclassifying the country [S0]. A weak rupiah raises imported input costs and imported-tile prices at the same time. Likelihood of continued illiquidity high, impact moderate; it lengthens the time to re-rating rather than changing the value.

Our scenarios mirror each other on the same two drivers. The bear cuts revenue growth by three points in every year and gross margin by five points, taking 31.7% to well below any year in the five-year record — the transfer-pricing, gas-quota and safeguard-lapse shock in one block — and values the stock at Rp561. The bull applies the same two shocks in the opposite direction, taking gross margin to just below the 36.9% actually earned in FY2023 and utilisation toward the level the annual report associates with full delivery of the housing programme, and values it at Rp1,150. The base case, at Rp802, assumes the fourth quarter repeats the third and margins hold at 31.7%. We weight bear and bull equally at 25.0% and 25.0% around a 50.0% base, which is the house default and also the honest reading: the evidence for the recovery is strong, the evidence for its persistence into the following year is not.

Two things about that table a reader should test us on. First, even the bear, at Rp561, is above the Rp505 price — by about a tenth. At 6.6x forward earnings on a net-cash balance sheet, the plausible downside is the absence of a re-rating rather than a loss of capital; a bear that goes below the price needs margins below anything in the five-year record and no recovery at all, which is a break-up case, not the most likely downside, and we will not dress it as one. Second, the bull is not a re-rating either: it is the FY2023 margin on capacity that is already bought, and it still sits below the FY2022 peak.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: renewal of the PGK-CSA sub-distributor agreements that expire on 31 December 2026 and carry more than four-fifths of sales; a gas quota decision that cuts industrial supply; the new year's housing target and first-quarter order flow; quarterly related-party receivables as a share of assets; renewal of the ceramic import safeguard; and the next gross margin print, where a figure below the FY2025 trough would say the recovery was a price spike rather than a mix shift [S3, S4, S6, S7, S8].

Arwana is controlled by its founder, Tandean Rustandy, with insiders holding 61.3% against a free float of 32.0%; the controlling stake is held directly rather than through a pyramidal group, and the company is not part of a conglomerate [S4, S0]. It is not on the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list, has not been deleted from an index, and has no enforcement action or special notation recorded against it [konglo registry]. The free float is comfortably above the minimum, so the rule change taking effect in 2027 does not force a placement [S0].

The related-party structure is the central governance fact. FY2025 sales to related parties were IDR2,427.0bn, more than four-fifths of consolidated net sales, and the largest customer — a related party — accounted for IDR1,981.8bn or roughly two-thirds of net sales; the group states that prices and terms are the same as for third parties, and the auditor's key-audit-matter paragraph shows the specific testing performed rather than a qualification [S3]. The counterparties are the Catur Sentosa group, appointed in writing as sub-distributors of the domestic ceramic range under an agreement running to the end of 2026, and the LK states that they are controlled by the same key management personnel as our own distribution subsidiary [S3]. That term expires on 31 December 2026, inside our twelve-month horizon: the base case assumes renewal on the disclosed terms, because more than four-fifths of FY2025 revenue — and roughly two-thirds through the single largest counterparty — passes through the channel, and we found no disclosure of what governs the relationship after that date [S3]. Receivables from related parties were IDR802.7bn, more than a quarter of total assets, down from just under a third the year before, so the trend is toward settlement rather than away from it [S3]. The minority in the distribution subsidiary means part of the channel profit leaves the group, which we carry in the model as a minority charge rather than as a governance penalty [S3, S0].

Disclosure and audit are conventional for a mid-cap. The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, an Ernst & Young member firm, which issued an unmodified opinion for FY2025 [S3, S4]. The board includes independent commissioners, and the annual report sets out the affiliation relationships between commissioners, directors and controlling shareholders [S4]. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the annual report, and we treat that as a checked negative rather than a confirmed clean bill.

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal: Rp55 in FY2022, Rp43 in each of the next two years and Rp45 for FY2025, paid out of cash generated by operations rather than by borrowing, with the payout rising from 69.4% in FY2022 to 71.6% in FY2024 and 79.0% in FY2025, and value returned through buy-backs on top [S0, S4, S2]. A controlling family that distributes that share of profit every year is not obviously extracting value through the profit and loss account; the risk is in the pricing of related-party flows, not in the dividend.

ESG exposure is concentrated in energy and emissions. Tile firing is gas-intensive, which makes the HGBT regime both a cost and a policy risk, and the company's environmental programme centres on certification under the ISO environmental management standard, Green Label Indonesia and industry-readiness assessments at its plants [S4]. Water and clay use are local-permit issues rather than group-level risks at this scale. The governance dimension, not the environmental one, is where a minority holder should focus.

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 results in March 2027, the first full year with the 75 million square metres capacity base, and the annual general meeting in April 2027 that sets the FY2026 dividend. Between now and then the HGBT volume-quota decision is the most important policy event for the cost base, and the new year's housing target in January sets the demand backdrop [S7, S8, S4].

The monthly and quarterly series we will track are: ASAKI national utilisation and capacity additions, which tell us whether the industry is growing into its 672 million square metres base or adding more idle capacity [S5]; the company's gross margin, the cleanest read on whether the rectified mix is holding [S2]; related-party receivables as a share of total assets, our governance tripwire [S3]; the trade ministry's safeguard and anti-dumping decisions [S6]; and the gas quota allocation [S7].

What would make us wrong: a fourth-quarter revenue print below the third, which would say the 2026 acceleration was a pull-forward; a gross margin below the FY2025 trough, which would say the mix shift is not structural; or a related-party receivable build that outgrows revenue, which would say the channel is being used to fund affiliates rather than to sell tiles [S2, S3].

bear.narrative: The related-party channel reprices against us and the import door reopens. A five-point gross-margin shift is the transfer-pricing shock the auditor's key audit matter flags, compounded by a gas quota cut and the safeguard lapsing: 31.7% becomes 26.7%, below every year in the five-year record, and revenue growth runs three points lower as the housing programme stalls [S3, S4, S6, S7].

bull.narrative: The housing programme delivers and the rectified/porcelain mix carries: a five-point gross-margin gain takes the margin to just below the 36.9% actually earned in FY2023 and still well below the FY2022 peak, while revenue growth is three points higher as 75m m2 is absorbed at higher utilisation with the capacity already bought [S4, S8, S0].

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is nine months of actual plus one quarter: net sales of Rp2,512.4bn in 9M2026 (+15.6% on 9M2025) with Q3 at Rp982.1bn, so FY2026E of Rp3,482bn assumes Q4 at ~Rp970bn, flat on Q3 and well above the weak 2025Q4 of Rp740bn [S2, S0]. From FY2027E the driver is capacity, not price: installed capacity reaches 75m m2 in 2026 against 68.0m m2 sold in 2025, so +4% volume plus ~3.5% ASP/mix (rectified share already 46% of output) gives ~7.5%, fading to 5.5% by FY2030E as the 75m m2 line is absorbed and national capacity grows to 728m m2 by 2029 [S4, S5]. LT 4.5% is below nominal GDP so no perpetual share gain is assumed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin is 31.7% (gross profit Rp796.1bn on Rp2,512.4bn) and Q3 alone 32.4%, up from 30.3% in FY2025 as the rectified/porselen mix rose to 46% of production and ASP outpaced gas and raw-material cost [S2, S4]. The base case holds 31.7-31.8% and never returns to the 40.7% of FY2022: the FY2023-FY2025 path (36.9%, 34.3%, 30.3%) is the evidence that gas prices and import competition compress the spread, so a recovery to the old peak would be unsourced [S0]. LT 31.5% keeps the margin at the last actual, not below it.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expenses are Rp294.8bn, 11.7% of net sales, against 12.2% in FY2025 and 13.6% in FY2024: fixed distribution and advertising costs spread over a larger volume [S2, S0]. The base holds 11.8-12.0%, i.e. the current run-rate with no further operating leverage claimed beyond the mix already visible.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 depreciation was Rp128.4bn (4.41% of revenue), FY2024 Rp111.9bn and FY2023 Rp112.6bn per the LK notes, not the Rp3.8bn the data pack carries [S3, S9, F1-F3]. Plant 4D adds 5.5m m2 of capacity and lifts the charge, so 4.4% in FY2026E rising to 4.8% as the capex programme (9-10% of sales) runs well above D&A.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex was Rp305.5bn (10.5% of revenue) and 9M2026 already Rp193.4bn, with Plant 4D (Ogan Ilir, 5.5m m2/yr) scheduled for completion in December 2026 and still under construction at the balance-sheet date [S3, S4, S2]. We hold 9.5% in FY2026E and fade to 8.0% from FY2029E, the level that funds the 4.5% LT revenue growth honestly: at D&A of 4.8% of revenue and working capital at 13.2%, reinvestment is about a quarter of NOPAT, so the terminal return on new capital is ~16% rather than the ~22% that a 7.0% capex would imply. That is the fade the method card requires of a fragmented, price-competitive industry, and 8.0% still sits inside the FY2023-FY2025 realised range of 7.5-10.5% [S0, S3].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was Rp384.2bn, 13.2% of revenue, down from 19.1% in FY2024 as receivables fell from Rp919bn to Rp885bn and inventories from Rp166bn to Rp119bn [S0]. The base holds the last actual 13.2% flat: no further release is claimed, and no deterioration is assumed.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 tax of Rp117.7bn on Rp523.6bn pre-tax profit is 22.5%, in line with the 22% corporate rate plus non-deductible items [S3, S0]. Held at 22.5%.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense of Rp7.4bn on opening debt of Rp107bn is 6.9%; the company is net cash (Rp2.3bn debt against Rp260bn cash at 30 September 2026), so this line is immaterial to value [S3, S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of Rp10.9bn on opening cash of Rp392bn is 2.8%; held at 3.0% for the forecast given the higher 2026 rate environment [S3, S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company repaid debt in every year of the history and holds Rp2.3bn of debt at 30 September 2026; no new borrowing is assumed [S0].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the FY2025 gap of Rp-8.1bn between EBIT plus net interest and pre-tax profit is FX and miscellaneous, not a recurring line, and nothing in the LK or the 2026 news flow makes it a forecast item [S3, S0].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is the 35% not owned of PGK, the distribution subsidiary; it took 1.3% of FY2025 net profit and 2.0% of 9M2026 profit [S3, S2, S0]. Held at 1.5%.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 was Rp45 a share against EPS of Rp56.97, a 79.0% payout, and the cash-flow statement shows Rp316.2bn of dividends paid in 2026 on parent profit of Rp400.5bn, 78.9% [S2, S0]. The announced ratio of 82.40% is struck on the issued share count and overstates the cash actually paid because treasury shares receive nothing [S11]. We hold 79%, the last actual, for every forecast year: capex of 9.5% of revenue is funded from operating cash flow of the same order, so nothing in the accounts says the payout steps down.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Treasury stock rose by Rp37.5bn in FY2025 and a further Rp36.0bn in the nine months to 30 September 2026, from Rp183.1bn to Rp219.0bn, against 7,341.4m shares issued and 311.5m held in treasury at end-2025 [S2, S4]. Outstanding shares fell from 7,271m in FY2022 to 7,030m in FY2025, about -1.1% a year, and the 2026 run-rate is at least that. We carry -1.1% a year, the realised average, rather than the faster 2026 pace.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.0% nominal, inside Indonesian long-run nominal GDP (5.3% real plus inflation in the macro deck) and below the 4.5% LT revenue growth, so the terminal year does not assume perpetual share gain [macro deck, S5].

challenges.challenge: F24 cites S11 for 2.333 gerai ritel dan 70 pusat distribusi as ARNA's own network, but in S11 that sentence sits in the ERAA (Erajaya, mobile phones) paragraph, immediately before the ARNA dividend paragraph; S4 p47 gives ARNA 56 sub-distributors and tens of thousands of stores and no such outlet count. The number is then used as the distribution-density moat in sections 1 and 2, and the same ERAA paragraph's management commentary is cited for channel breadth as ARNA's principal defence.
challenges.answer: F24 replaced with the ARNA-sourced sub-distributor count (49 to 56, S4 p.68) and the ERAA outlet/depot claim deleted from the business text, the moat and the terminal argument; the moat now rests on 97% utilisation against 73% for the industry and the sub-distributor network [S4].

challenges.challenge: The bear shifts only revenue growth by -3pp and gross margin by -1.5pp, giving Rp722, which is 43% above the Rp505 price. The four risks section 5 rates impact high (related-party pricing, gas quota, safeguard lapse, related-party receivables) are unmodelled, so no scenario shows a loss and the BUY cannot be stress-tested for downside.
challenges.answer: Bear now shocks margin as well as growth: five points off gross margin and three points off revenue growth, mirrored in the bull; the bear value is Rp561 against a Rp505 price, within a tenth, at a stated 25% probability [S3, S4, S6, S7].

challenges.challenge: 83.3% of FY2025 revenue is related-party and 68.0% is to CSA alone (S3 pp6, 95-97); Rp802.7bn of related-party receivables is about 28% of total assets. The report calls this optics-class and priced, but nothing in the model prices it: both multiples are peer medians and the WACC is at the band floor. A 5pp gross-margin shift to the affiliate cuts FY2026E EBIT by roughly Rp174bn.
challenges.answer: The related-party channel is now priced explicitly: a 50bp governance premium lifts the cost of equity and WACC inside the band, the bear case takes five points of gross margin (about Rp174bn of FY2026E gross profit), and both cross-checks stay at peer medians rather than a premium [S3].

challenges.challenge: The bull adds only 3pp growth and 1.5pp gross margin, while the base holds 31.7% gross margin flat for ten years even though 9M2026 is already 31.7%, Q3 is 32.4%, FY2021-22 ran 36-41%, and the Ogan Ilir line is large-format porcelain, the highest-margin product. The sensitivity table says +1pp gross margin is worth about Rp44 and +2pp growth about Rp90.
challenges.answer: Bull widened to five points of gross margin and three points of growth, to just below the 36.9% actually earned in FY2023; the base is not understated because it starts at the 31.7% nine-month actual and the FY2023-FY2025 slide is the evidence against a return to the FY2022 peak [S2, S0, S4].

challenges.challenge: The cash-return lever is in no scenario: net cash of Rp257.7bn is 7% of the Rp3.55tn market cap, the forward yield is 11.5%, payout was 82.4% of FY2025 profit (S11) and buybacks continued into 2026 (treasury Rp183.1bn to Rp219.0bn by 30 June 2026, S2). The base assumes 76% payout and a -0.5% share count.
challenges.answer: Payout raised to the 79% last actual and the share count cut at the realised 1.1% a year, so the cash-return path is in the base: section 3 shows FY2027E earnings per share growing faster than net profit, with the gap being the buy-back [S2, S11, S0].

challenges.challenge: Payout of 76% and share change of -0.5% are both below the last actual (80.5% of EPS and 82.4% of profit; -1.1% a year), and neither cited source says the company intends to slow buybacks - S2 shows treasury stock rising by Rp36bn in H1 2026. FY2027E volume growth of 4% is also half the 9.4% capacity headroom (75.0 vs 68.8m m2).
challenges.answer: Both inputs now sit at the last actual: 79% payout against 80.5% of EPS, and a 1.1% a year share reduction against treasury stock rising in 2026; volume is reconciled as 75m m2 of capacity at 97% utilisation, about seven percent above 68.0m m2 sold [S2, S4, S0].

challenges.challenge: The section 4 WACC build does not reproduce 11.18%: 7.45% + 0.80 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 12.80%, because the engine silently subtracts a 1.62% default spread. The rate is at the floor of the 11-13% band and no governance premium is applied anywhere, although sections 4 and 6 say the related-party risk is carried in the discount rate.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now reproduces the engine: risk-free less the Indonesia default spread, plus levered beta times mature ERP plus country risk, plus a 50bp governance premium, giving 11.68%; the premium is sourced to the 83.29% related-party revenue and 27.90% related-party receivables [S3].

challenges.challenge: 55.3% of the DCF is terminal value on FY2035 FCFF of Rp689bn growing 4% forever, implying a ~22% perpetual ROIIC (reinvestment ~18% of NOPAT) against an 11.2% WACC. Section 4 says the terminal gross margin below the last actual means no perpetual excess return is capitalised, which does not follow. The implied exit is 7.35x EV/EBITDA against 5.0x LTM and 3.9x forward.
challenges.answer: Life capex raised to 8.0% of sales so terminal reinvestment is about a quarter of NOPAT and terminal return on new capital about 16% against an 11.68% WACC; terminal value share falls to 52.2%, and section 4 now gives the no-moat values (P/E cross-check and bear case) against the DCF [S0, S4].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 5.63x to an LTM EBITDA of Rp633.8bn that is LTM EBIT of Rp630.0bn plus the pack's Rp3.8bn D&A - the exact error section 3 restates out of the model lines. Restated LTM EBITDA is roughly Rp760-770bn, so the Rp538 cross-check is about 8% low and section 4's explanation that it capitalises trough LTM earnings does not apply to it.
challenges.answer: Rebuilding LTM EBITDA from restated D&A requires the engine restatement hook, which replaces the whole LTM block with FY2025 and drops September-2026 net profit, costing about Rp22 a share on the P/E leg; section 4 discloses the stale charge, calls the cross-check a floor and sizes the correction at about a fifth of its value [S0, S3].

challenges.challenge: Sells roughly a fifth of national output contradicts section 1's own 66.9m m2 against 672m m2 capacity is roughly a tenth, and at the report's 73% utilisation national output is ~490m m2 so ARNA is ~14%. The largest listed Indonesian ceramic-tile producer is also uncited and not checked against listed tile peers.
challenges.answer: Summary corrected to about a seventh of national output, consistent with 66.9m m2 of production against 672m m2 of national capacity at 73% utilisation; the uncited largest listed producer claim is replaced by leader among listed peers but not dominant [S4, S5].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex of Rp330.9bn (9.5% of sales) against 9M actual of Rp193.4bn implies Rp137.5bn in Q4, above FY2025's Q4 of Rp117.6bn and nearly double the 9M quarterly average of Rp64.5bn, with no source tying the step-up to Plant 4D completion payments.
challenges.answer: Capex held at 9.5% of FY2026E sales because the September accounts carry Plant 4D as work in progress three-quarters to four-fifths complete with completion scheduled for December 2026, so the payment falls in the fourth quarter [S2, S4].

missing_bull_case.note: The bull adds only 3pp growth and 1.5pp gross margin on a DCF whose sensitivity is worth ~Rp90/share per 2pp of growth, while the base holds 31.7% gross margin flat for a decade despite 9M2026 already at 31.7% and Q3 at 32.4%. Capacity (75.0 vs 68.8m m2), the 11.5% forward yield and the continuing buyback are in no scenario.

missing_bear_case.note: All four risks rated impact high in section 5 are absent from the bear: 83.3% related-party revenue and 68% to CSA alone (S3 pp6, 95-97), the HGBT quota, a safeguard lapse and Rp802.7bn of related-party receivables (28% of assets). The bear value of Rp722 is still 43% above the Rp505 price, so no scenario shows a loss.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue and margin drivers reconcile to 9M2026 (2,512.4 / 796.1 / 369.6bn, S2) and are defensible, but FY2027E volume of +4% is half the 9.4% capacity headroom, payout (76%) and share change (-0.5%) sit below the last actual, and Q3 standalone data come from Yahoo quarterly (S0), not the 9M filing.

evidence_and_citations.note: Verified: D&A 128.4/111.9/112.6bn (S3 p57, S9), related-party revenue 83.29% (S3 p6), CSA 68.0% (S3 p95/97), 97% utilisation and 46% rectified (S4 pp39, 67), 9M2026 P&L and Rp260.0bn cash (S2), 1.79m housing units (S8). F24's 2,333 outlets is ERAA's, from the same S11 page, and is misattributed.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF is the right primary method, but the section 4 WACC build (7.4% + 0.8 x 6.7% = 12.8%) does not reproduce 11.18% because the engine subtracts an undisclosed 1.62% spread; the rate is at the 11-13% band floor with zero governance premium; 55.3% of value is a no-fade terminal at ~22% perpetual ROIIC; EV/EBITDA uses a stale LTM EBITDA.

bias_and_tone.note: The summary's 'roughly a fifth of national output' contradicts section 1's own 'a tenth of the installed base', and at 73% utilisation ARNA is ~14%. 'Largest listed producer' is uncited. 'Disclosed, audited and priced' asserts a discount that appears nowhere in the model; section 4's 'no perpetual excess return' claim is arithmetically false.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: No commodity deck applies because ceramic tiles have no exchange benchmark, and the macro deck is used consistently (5.3% real GDP and 3.3% CPI inside the 4.0% terminal, USD/IDR and the policy rate in the demand discussion). The peer set is the INDUSTRIAL_GOODS basket with no direct tile comparable, and that limitation is disclosed.

conservatism_audit.note: Below the last actual without a source that says so: payout 76% vs 80.5% of EPS and 82.4% of profit (S11); share change -0.5% vs -1.1% a year actual, with treasury stock rising from Rp183.1bn to Rp219.0bn in H1 2026 (S2); FY2027E volume +4% vs +9.4% capacity headroom; terminal g 4.0% vs ~8.6% nominal GDP; terminal gross margin 31.5% vs 31.7%. Individually small, the stack is worth roughly 5-8% of the target.

calibration.note: qc is clean apart from extreme_call, whose justification cites the 9M2026 actuals, the 75m m2 capacity and the 6.6x forward P/E and is adequate. The 1.82pp calibration gap is FY2026E margin against FY2025A and is the sourced 9M2026 recovery, not an unsourced drift; FY+1 reproduces the last actual at last-year prices within that gap.

signoff.notes: The 2026 recovery is already in the accounts (9M2026 revenue +15.6%, gross margin 31.7%), the base holds the last actual working capital of 13.2% and the 31.7% margin, WACC 11.68% sits inside the 11-13% band with the governance premium, and g 4.0% is below nominal GDP. C1 FATAL (the ERAA-sourced distribution claim) and C2-C11 are answered on substance, and the related-party channel of 83% of sales, 68% to one affiliate, is disclosed and priced three ways (premium, bear margin shock, peer median multiples). The EV/EBITDA floor is disclosed as a floor. Approve.

bias.note: Base case holds the 9M2026 actuals (gross margin 31.7%, opex 11.7%), the last cash payout (79.0%) and the realised -1.1% share count; FY2027-30 volume growth of ~4%/yr is below the ~7% capacity headroom; bear and bull mirror the same two drivers (-3pp/+3pp growth, -5pp/+5pp gross margin) at 25/25 around a 50% base, so there is no unsupported conservatism or optimism on either side.

findings.finding: Section 3 writes the treasury buy-back share count as IDR7,271.2bn to IDR7,030.0bn; these are share counts (7,271.2m to 7,030.0m shares), not rupiah amounts.

Section 4 uses a 9.4% pre-tax cost of debt while the cost_of_debt input basis derives 6.9% (7.0% input); immaterial at a 0.06% debt weight and the WACC reproduces at 11.7%, but the two should agree. Judge raised the same point.

The 15%-weighted EV/EBITDA cross-check still capitalises LTM EBITDA of Rp633.8bn, which omits the restated D&A; a restated ~Rp760bn lifts the method from Rp538 to about Rp647 and the target by ~2%. It is disclosed as a floor in section 4.
The valuation bridge deducts Rp42.6bn of minorities against the Rp37.9bn NCI book value at 30 September 2026 [S2 note 16]; the effect is under Rp1 a share.
The summary and section 1 pair the 75m m2 2026 capacity with the 97% utilisation, which is the FY2025 rate on the pre-expansion base; 68.0m m2 sold against 75m m2 is 91%.

flags.message: expected return +76%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers produce the return. First, the 2026 recovery is already in the accounts, not a forecast: 9M2026 net sales of Rp2,512.4bn (+15.6% on 9M2025) with gross profit of Rp796.1bn and profit to owners of Rp369.6bn against Rp302.1bn a year earlier [S2]. Second, capacity: 75m m2 installed in 2026 after the Ogan Ilir line against 68.0m m2 sold in FY2025, so volume and rectified mix (46% of output) can grow without new capital [S4]. Third, the price: at Rp505 the stock is on 6.6x FY2026E earnings and 3.9x EV/EBITDA on a net-cash balance sheet paying out three quarters of profit; running the DCF backwards at that price solves for zero revenue growth, i.e. the market capitalises no recovery at all [S0, S3].
